name: Erik Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. Walk me through an ordinary day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead a group of customer service supervisors in a large company. I have an MBA, but most of the day is less grand than that sounds: the morning rota, escalated calls, overtime records, and coaching a lead who has just had a rough shift. I like helping someone get a fair hearing; I hate seeing the cost freeze turn vacant posts into permanent extra work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is work like after you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is between short contracts, so I cover most of our flat and we watch the cash account. We've got about three months of expenses saved, and there are a few comparable manager jobs nearby, but I won't pretend an outside offer would arrive overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the customer service leads that a faster rota is fine if somebody still listens when a caller has been bounced around. I'd also say no one should be judged by a machine-generated score they can't challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the stable picture doesn't erase our cost freeze; my partner is between contracts and I cover most of the flat. I've got about three months of expenses saved, which helps, but it isn't a reason to stop watching the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now I'll keep running the morning staffing huddle with the same spreadsheet and ask payroll to show how any automatic scores are checked. In the first year of this plateau, I'll hold back 120 a month in our cash account and renew the team training schedule rather than replace it with a tool I haven't tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm mostly steady about my role, but our household income still feels tight. A small software change can still become an excuse to squeeze the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has the cost freeze meant for your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost two open posts last spring, so the remaining supervisors cover more escalations. I spend lunch with Priya from payroll checking whether the overtime numbers actually match what people worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a new scoring tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need staff to see the inputs and an appeal that reaches a person with authority. I won't use AI myself to decide whether a colleague did enough; I don't use those tools now.

say: I'd accept a **faster rota** if people can still hear and fix a customer complaint.
I'd challenge any **automatic score** that workers cannot inspect or appeal.
think: Our **cost freeze** and my partner's uncertain contracts already put pressure on household income.
Three months of savings give us room, but the two unfilled posts mean **staff pressure** remains.
do: Run the **morning huddle** from the current spreadsheet and ask payroll how automatic scores are checked.
Set aside **120 monthly** and keep the team training schedule through the first year.
feel: **Mostly steady** about my post, with household money still tight.
S0.quote: A small software change can still become an excuse to squeeze the staff.
fieldNote: The **cost freeze** predates the AI story; his partner's uncertain work makes the household cautious.
He questions automated measures through **payroll records** and an appeal process, not through personal use of AI.

steps.text: Run the morning staffing huddle from the current spreadsheet
Set aside 120 monthly in the household cash account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption needs a written agreement about retraining and how performance scores are used. Planning and customer replies are the first things our company will hand to software, and our leads deserve a say before roles are merged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry that my skill at coaching supervisors becomes invisible if the dashboard claims to do the planning. The company has already left two posts empty; it could call the next cut 'natural turnover' and still strip my team of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd bring the open-post figures to our staff council and ask for a meeting with HR about role changes. In the first year of steady disruption, I'd ask HR for paid time to train in difficult customer cases and take the course if they fund it. I'd keep a dated log of what the software gets wrong before anyone's score is used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about being the one who has to tell a supervisor their job vanished. I can deal with changes if they are argued in daylight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask HR to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether vacant lead jobs will be filled and whether training hours are paid. I'd also ask for an appeal route before automatic scores go into reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want new training but avoid AI tools. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn a better way to handle a hard case without letting a text generator write my judgment. If a tool has to be used, I want someone else to show it works before I rely on it.

say: I'd press for a **written agreement** on paid retraining and automatic performance scores.
I'd tell leads that **planning and replies** may be handed to software before roles are merged.
think: My **coaching work** may vanish from what a dashboard measures, even if supervisors still need it.
Unfilled posts make another **quiet cut** credible without a formal redundancy notice.
do: Bring **vacancy figures** to the staff council this month and seek an HR meeting.
Take **case training** if HR funds the time, and log software errors in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about telling a supervisor their post has gone.
S1.quote: I can deal with changes if they are argued in daylight.
fieldNote: He frames public demands around **paid time**, vacancies and appeals rather than a blanket rejection of software.
He will retrain in **customer cases** but waits for evidence before he personally relies on an AI tool.

steps.text: Take the two unfilled lead posts to the staff council
Take difficult-customer training if HR funds the time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 calls for a joint meeting with staff representatives before any team plan is approved. A system that can do nearly all the thinking work puts the rotas, complaint replies and my own manager role in play, even if robots wait until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think my MBA or my record as a lead protects me if the company buys cheaper thinking work. My partner's contract could end at the same time, and three months of savings would go quickly if both paychecks stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'd ask the staff council to demand a freeze on cuts until workers see the plan, and I'd cut our nonessential spending by 200 a month. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post goes, I'd check whether we qualify for job-loss support and claim it only if eligible, then apply for employee-relations jobs in the neighboring city, taking a bus before considering a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed because two salaries could disappear inside one lease term. I still have a list of steps, but I don't believe the company will volunteer what it plans to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending goes first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend trips and takeaway meals go first; the rent and my partner's travel to interviews don't. I'd rather have an awkward conversation now than a missed payment in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your supervisors at that joint meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I can't promise protection, only a chance to see the numbers and challenge a bad plan. If I asked for trust while hiding the staffing sheet, I would deserve none.

say: I'd demand a **joint staff meeting** before a 2028 team plan is approved.
I'd warn that **rotas, replies and management** are exposed before robots arrive in 2031.
think: My **MBA and lead record** may not protect a post built on thinking work.
If both household incomes stop, **three months saved** will run down quickly.
do: Ask the **staff council** for a pause on cuts until workers see the plan.
Cut **200 monthly** in trips and meals; seek neighboring-city employee-relations work if cut after 2028.
Check **job-loss eligibility** and claim support only if eligible.
feel: **Alarmed** by the risk of losing both paychecks within one lease term.
S2.quote: If I asked for trust while hiding the staffing sheet, I would deserve none.
fieldNote: His **staff council request** follows a concrete fear: company decisions could outpace worker notice.
He separates **2028 thinking work** from 2031 robots and keeps bus commuting ahead of moving home.

steps.text: Ask the staff council to seek a pause on cuts before 2028
Cut weekend trips and takeaway meals by 200 monthly
Apply for employee-relations posts in the neighboring city if cut after 2028
Check job-loss support eligibility and claim only if eligible after his post ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff council that AGI by 2031 gives us time to bargain for training and a clear path out of roles the company expects to remove. I wouldn't call five years generous, but I would ask for annual staffing numbers rather than a last-minute announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build six months of savings before 2031 if my partner's work steadies, and I might be able to move toward employee relations. The software would still reach my reporting and planning on the 2031 date, not wait for the robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in January, I'd take an evening course in workplace mediation, which means helping two sides settle a dispute. If my partner's contracts steady, I'd also save another 180 each month. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for internal employee-relations roles first and look at nearby employers if those posts are also cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy and busy, not frozen. There's enough time to prepare if the training is real and the jobs it leads to exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that course worth the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to shadow our employee-relations adviser on actual grievance meetings, not just collect a certificate. A paper course with no practice won't persuade another employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you agree to use AI in the new role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let a tested system file meeting notes if everyone consented and a person checked the record. I would not let it tell me whose grievance is true.

say: I'd bargain for **paid training** and yearly staffing numbers ahead of 2031.
I'd ask for a **clear route** out of posts the company expects to remove.
think: Six months of **savings** might be possible if my partner's contracts become steadier.
My **planning work** changes in 2031; robots three years later do not extend my deadline.
do: Save another **180 monthly** from January if my partner's work steadies, and take an evening mediation course.
Seek **employee-relations posts** inside the company after 2031, then at nearby employers if needed.
feel: **Uneasy and busy**, with some control if training connects to real vacancies.
S3.quote: A paper course with no practice won't persuade another employer.
fieldNote: The longer runway moves him from **emergency cuts** to savings and a practical career shift.
He remains wary of AI judgment but could accept **checked notes** with everyone's consent.

steps.text: Save another 180 monthly from January if partner contracts steady
Take an evening course in workplace mediation
Apply for internal employee-relations posts after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 means our company should fund a long transition agreement now, with figures checked every year. A decade is enough to train people for new roles if employers stop treating training as a favor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 at the thinking-AI date, and I don't want ten years of managing a shrinking team on a familiar spreadsheet. I could make a real career in employee relations by then, but I'd need to know the roles are there before betting our savings on a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep mentoring the current supervisors and ask the staff council for a yearly report on roles removed and created. Over the decade I'd seek a paid secondment into employee relations and take it if the company funds the placement. In the first year after 2036, I'd stay if that work still has people and authority behind it, or apply elsewhere with the experience I'd built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously hopeful about the time, though the current cost freeze still bothers me. Ten years only helps if we check the promises each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on a secondment instead of an outside application now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see the grievance work before leaving a job I know how to do. My partner has enough uncertainty in contract work without both of us making a blind jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in the yearly report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the number of lead posts, paid training places and actual transfers, not just the company's course completions. A training place that leads nowhere is a polite way to make us wait.

say: I'd seek a **transition agreement** with yearly figures and funded training before 2036.
I'd tell the company **ten years** is enough to offer real routes into other roles.
think: At **37**, I could have a career in employee relations, if those jobs still exist.
Our current **cost freeze** means I won't gamble household savings on an untested move.
do: Keep **mentoring supervisors** this year and request yearly role counts through the staff council.
Take a **paid secondment** before 2036 if offered; decide then whether to stay or apply elsewhere.
feel: **Cautiously hopeful**, while wary of promises that are never checked.
S4.quote: A training place that leads nowhere is a polite way to make us wait.
fieldNote: He uses the decade to pursue a **low-risk secondment** rather than a sudden career jump.
The **existing cost freeze** and partner's contract income keep him concerned even on the longest runway.

steps.text: Keep mentoring the current customer service supervisors this year
Ask the staff council for yearly counts of lead posts and transfers
Take an employee-relations secondment before 2036 if the company funds it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most: our planning and customer replies could change before we have any agreement on jobs, and both incomes might be at risk. A negotiated staffing plan, paid training tied to real openings, and job-loss support would give us more than a speech about opportunity.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who gets to inspect the numbers behind a cut. My supervisors can't challenge a decision if even I haven't been shown the staffing sheet.

headlineQuote: My supervisors can't challenge a decision if even I haven't been shown the staffing sheet.
portrait: At **27**, Erik leads customer service supervisors at a large company and holds an MBA.
His **three-month cushion** helps, but a cost freeze and his partner's short contracts keep household income uncertain.
He avoids **AI tools** and seeks evidence, appeals and paid training before relying on company systems.
A 2028 arrival triggers **staff bargaining** and home cuts; longer runways allow mediation training and a secondment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his planning role before staff agree on terms, while his partner's income also wavers.
whatWouldHelp: A **negotiated staffing plan**, paid training linked to jobs and job-loss support would help his household prepare.
